title: How to Massage Your Feet: A 10-Minute Foot Massage at Home — cv.cm
description: Foot massage at home: a safe warm soak, thumb walking, toe pulls, arch and heel work, ankle circles, a ball roll and a 10-minute routine.
h1: How do you give a foot massage at home?
answer: Soak the feet in warm, not hot, water for about 10 minutes, dry them well, and warm a little lotion or oil in your hands. Glide over the whole foot, walk your thumbs along the sole, knead the arch, press the heel, gently pull each toe and circle the ankle. Ten minutes for both feet is enough. Keep pressure firm but comfortable.

sections.h: Before you start: a safe warm soak
body: A warm soak is optional but makes feet feel relaxed and the skin softer. It is also part of the foot massage tradition in many places, from foot massage shops in China, Taiwan and Vietnam to home foot baths in Japan and Korea.

ol: Fill a basin with lukewarm water, about body temperature.
Test the water with your hand or elbow before putting your feet in, never with your foot.
Soak for about 10 minutes. Longer soaks dry the skin.
Dry the feet completely, including between the toes.

body.note: If you have diabetes or numb feet, you may not feel water that is too hot. MedlinePlus advises washing the feet in lukewarm water, checking the temperature with your hand or elbow first, not using a heating pad or hot water bottle on the feet, and checking the feet every day. Do not put lotion or oil between the toes.

body: Oil or lotion: a small amount, about half a teaspoon per foot, of plain, unscented lotion or oil. Lotion suits feet well because it absorbs. Wipe off extra oil before standing up, because oily feet slip on the floor.
Hold the foot with both hands, fingers on top and thumbs on the sole. Most of the work is done by the thumbs, so rest them often.

body: Work around the ankle bones, not on them, and stay gentle on the top of the foot, where bones and tendons sit just under the skin.
Do steps 2 to 7 on one foot, then repeat on the other. For example, cv.cm's countdown timer can time each step so both feet get equal time.

body: Self-massage: sit on a chair or the floor and rest one foot on the opposite thigh. You will have less leverage than when massaging someone else, so use your knuckles for the arch and heel.

sections.h: Rolling a ball under the foot
body: Rolling the sole over a ball is an easy way to massage your own feet, even at work.

ol: Sit on a chair with a tennis ball, or a firmer massage ball, on the floor under one foot.
Roll the ball slowly from the heel to the ball of the foot and back for about 1 minute.
Pause on any tender spot for 20–30 seconds, pressing at about 4–5 out of 10.
For more pressure, stand up and hold a chair or wall for balance. Switch feet.

body: Many people with heel or arch tightness like this. The NHS advises gentle stretches of the sole and heel, supportive shoes, rest and ice for plantar fasciitis, a common cause of heel pain. See a doctor if heel pain is severe, gets worse, keeps coming back or has not improved after 2 weeks of self-care, or if you have tingling or loss of feeling in the foot, or diabetes and foot pain.

ul: Raise your feet on a cushion or stool for 10–15 minutes before or after the massage.
Roll a ball under each foot for 1–2 minutes during breaks.
Do ten slow ankle circles each way and ten toe curls with each foot.
Gently stretch the calf: stand facing a wall, one foot back, heel down, and lean forward until you feel a stretch. Hold 20–30 seconds.
Choose supportive, cushioned shoes for long days on your feet.

body: Swelling in both ankles after a long day is common and should go down overnight. Swelling that does not go down, or is only in one leg, should be checked by a doctor.

sections.h: What the evidence says about foot massage and reflexology
body: Many people find a foot massage relaxing, and that is a good reason to do one. There is little research on plain foot massage itself.

Reflexology is a different idea: it holds that points on the feet correspond to other parts of the body. NCCIH says claims of relaxation and healing effects from reflexology have not been proven, and evidence for specific conditions is limited. The reflexology foot chart is a traditional map, not anatomy. You do not need it for a relaxing foot massage, and you should never use it to judge whether an organ is unwell.

sections.h: Safety: when not to massage the feet

ul: Skip any area with a cut, blister, ulcer, athlete's foot, a wart, an infected toenail or a fresh bruise.
Do not massage a foot or ankle that is swollen, hot and painful after an injury, such as a sprain, or a toe or foot that may be broken.

Never massage a calf that is swollen, warm, red or painful on one side. It can be a sign of a blood clot (DVT). Contact a doctor the same day, and call emergency services if it comes with chest pain or shortness of breath.
Diabetes or numb feet: gentle pressure only, no hot water, check the skin before and after, and see your doctor about any wound that is not healing.
Varicose veins in the lower legs: light gliding only around them, no deep pressure.
Blood thinners or a bleeding disorder: gentle pressure only.
Pregnancy: ask a midwife or doctor before foot massage. Traditional acupressure advice avoids firm pressure on `SP6` above the inner ankle.

body: Mistakes and fixes: if the feet are sore the next day, halve the pressure and time. If your thumbs hurt, switch to knuckles or the heel of your hand. If the foot feels ticklish, use firmer, slower strokes rather than light ones.

faq.q: Is it good to massage your feet every day?
faq.a: For most healthy adults a gentle 5–10 minute foot massage every day is fine. Skip any area that is sore, injured or has broken skin.

faq.q: Should I use oil or lotion for a foot massage?
faq.a: Lotion is usually easier because it absorbs and leaves the feet less slippery. If you use oil, wipe off the extra before walking, and avoid putting either between the toes if you have diabetes.

faq.q: Can foot massage help plantar fasciitis?
faq.a: Some people find rolling a ball under the foot and stretching the sole comfortable. It is not a treatment on its own, and heel pain that has not improved after 2 weeks of self-care should be checked by a doctor.

faq.q: Why are my feet so sensitive when massaged?
faq.a: The soles have many nerve endings, so light touch often tickles. Slow, firmer pressure with the whole thumb or hand usually feels better than light fingertip strokes.

faq.q: Can people with diabetes have a foot massage?
faq.a: Often yes, but gently. Check the feet for cuts or blisters first, avoid hot water, keep lotion away from between the toes, and ask your doctor if you have nerve damage or foot wounds.
